title: The Math of Takeoff: Returns, Reproduction Number and Ceilings

questions.question: In the simplest software-only feedback model, progress per cycle is ΔL = k · S^(a − 1/r). With full automation (a = 1), which condition makes the growth rate itself grow over time?
options: r < 1, because weaker diminishing returns let each cycle's research go further
k > 1, because a first cycle that gains more than one OOM keeps the rate rising
r > 1, because each doubling of research then buys more than one doubling of S
a = 0, because fixed research input cannot be diluted by rising difficulty
questions.explanation: With a = 1 the exponent is (r − 1)/r, which is positive exactly when r > 1; then each OOM of progress makes the next cycle's gain larger. k only scales the curve and a = 0 removes the feedback entirely.

questions.question: Davidson and Houlden (Forethought, Aug 2025) estimate 6–16 OOMs of software-efficiency headroom after ASARA. Why does that make 'ten years of progress in one year' hard?
options: At ~10× effective compute per year, ten years is ~10 OOMs, so limits must be >10 OOMs away
Each OOM takes a full year of wall-clock training time however good the software becomes
Ten OOMs of gain would require more than ten independent actors sharing every improvement
The headroom figure covers hardware only, and software progress is capped near 3 OOMs
questions.explanation: Their unit convention equates one year of recent progress with roughly one OOM of effective compute, so ten years-in-one needs ten OOMs of software gains, which is impossible if the effective limit is closer than that.

questions.question: Burtsev's recursive reproduction number R_AI (arXiv:2609.00137) is best described as:
options: The benchmark score at which a model begins to improve itself without any human help
The number of model generations a lab can train per year at a fixed compute budget
The ratio of years of 2024-rate progress achieved to calendar years actually elapsed
Recursive feedback strength divided by growth in research difficulty; above 1, gains compound
questions.explanation: R_AI compares how strongly each cycle's improvement feeds the next cycle's research with how much harder the next step has become. It is a property of the loop's structure, not a capability level or a speed.

questions.question: In the simulator with a human baseline (b = 1, r = 1.2), R_AI crosses 1 at cycle 3 while the progress rate is 0.72× its start, and the rate does not double until cycle 13. Which of Burtsev's conclusions does this illustrate?
options: Rising research difficulty can end a period of self-amplification before anyone notices it
Self-amplification can begin well before any acceleration is visible in the progress curve
Baseline productivity shifts the criticality threshold, so removing humans is what matters
Cycle duration stops mattering once the loop is supercritical, so the lag is an artefact
questions.explanation: The loop is already supercritical at cycle 3 but the observable rate is still falling; ten cycles pass before the acceleration shows. Baseline productivity changes speed, not the asymptotic criticality.

questions.question: Two labs each feed back a = 0.6 of their improvements at r = 1.2, so each alone has a · r = 0.72. If improvements leak freely between them, what does Burtsev's framework predict?
options: The ecosystem can be supercritical although neither actor is, since shared feedback adds up
Nothing changes, because criticality is fixed by each actor's own research difficulty growth
The ecosystem turns subcritical, since sharing halves the gains each actor keeps for itself
Criticality depends only on the compute budget, so the sharing fraction cannot move it
questions.explanation: Sharing raises the effective feedback exponent of the ecosystem toward the sum of the parts, so the combined loop can cross R_AI = 1 while every individual actor stays below it.

questions.question: Which measurement would most directly distinguish genuine recursive amplification from fast progress driven by compute or human effort?
options: The absolute benchmark score of the newest model release compared with last year's release
The lab's total training compute in FLOP together with its year-over-year growth rate
Feedback strength and carry-over: how much of the next cycle's research input comes from this one
The number of research papers the lab publishes per quarter, weighted by their citations
questions.explanation: Burtsev's indicators are feedback strength, carry-over into successors, cycle duration and difficulty growth. Scores, compute and paper counts measure speed or inputs, not whether gains compound through the loop.
